attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click the palette to select a background image for this project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it useful to comment code, particularly when using JavaScript?

❓ What else might go in the // set up code? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Code comments make it easier to organize code and identify specific parts of a program. This is especially useful in JavaScript when there are no longer “containers” to visually separate code.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can click the arrow, to the right of the line number, to minimize the code for an image.
steps.instructions:
Set the stage for the performance by adding a background image to this project. 


Notice the code comment // set up on line 1 of the editor. In JavaScript // signals a code comment and the slashes and text will appear in green. This text will be skipped over when the project is run.


Open Scene, drag [set background image to (img)] under the comment // set up, on line 2 of the editor. 


Click the palette to the left of the line of code to choose the stage background image from the Gallery.


Click ▶ to see the background image appear in the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type quotation marks around the string inside the parentheses of game.splash(text)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What did the parameter look like in the [splash] block in the blocks editor? What symbols were already present in the text parameter?

❓ What might you splash on the screen at the beginning of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that in JavaScript, quotation marks must be placed around the string argument; without them, the project will not be able to run. Remind the ninja that [splash] in the blocks editor automatically adds the quotation marks in (and that they cannot be deleted), for this reason.
steps.instructions:
Add a short introduction message to the project. 


Open Game, drag [splash (title)] underneath the background image code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

game.splash(null)

Replace null with a string inside of quotation marks that shares an introduction message, like “Show time!”. Remember to include quotation marks when typing a string, otherwise the code will not be able to run!


Click ▶ to see the message appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the sprite’s name in the mySprite.setPosition(x, y) and update the y parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you format a sprite’s name in camelCase?

❓ Which argument moves the sprite left and right on the screen? Which argument moves the sprite up and down on the screen? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that camelCase replaces spaces in text with capital letters.

💡 As needed, the ninja can toggle back to blocks to use the visual coordinate grid to help them place a sprite in their desired location.
steps.instructions:
Add a sprite and set its starting position! 


Open Sprites, drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath the comment // sprite code, then click the palette to select a sprite. Replace mySprite by typing a new sprite name using camelCase. Give the sprite a simple name that describes what it is, such as actorSprite.


Open Sprites, drag out [set (mySprite) position to x y] on a blank line under the sprite set up code. Replace mySprite with the sprite’s name. Inside the parentheses, keep the x position set to 0 so that the sprite is placed on the left edge of the screen, then replace the second argument (0) with a number between 0 and 120 for the y position. 


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the sprite’s name in the mySprite.vx = value code and update the value for pixels per second?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should actorSprite.vx = 30 be typed out, instead of dragged from the menu?

❓ What other properties do you recognize from the code completion tool? Which block have you noticed them in before?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that not all of the blocks that were in the blocks editor menu appear as available code blocks in the JavaScript editor menu. When programming simple math equations or assigning a sprite property, the ninja will have to directly type out the code when using JavaScript. 

💡 Point out the connection to the ninja between the list of properties and those that can be found in the drop down menu in the [set sprite [x]] block. By using the dot operator ., the ninja can easily assign a wide variety of properties (including x, y, vx, vy, ax, ay, etc.) to a sprite.
steps.instructions:
Set the sprite’s velocity x (vx) to move it to center stage!


Instead of dragging out code like in previous steps, this code will be typed. On a line below the sprite’s existing code, type the name of the sprite, from the previous step, followed by a dot operator. 


Typing a dot will open a code completion tool that includes functions () and properties (). Find and select vx to add the property to the end of the sprite name in the code editor. Type = 30 to set the sprite’s vx to 30 pixels per second. The code will look like actorSprite.vx = 30



Click ▶ to see the sprite move across the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a pause(ms) and change the sprite’s velocity to 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does adding a pause to the code allow the sprite to stop at the center of the stage?

❓ What value should the argument be set to, so that the sprite stops at the right position?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the pause causes the program to stop running for the amount of time indicated in the parameter. However, the code that appears before the pause will continue to run. 

💡 Walk the ninja through the code logic: set mySprite’s vx to 30. Stop running the rest of the code for 3 seconds, while mySprite is still moving. After 3 seconds, set mySprite’s vx to 0, stopping the sprite in its current position.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The sprite keeps moving past the spotlight and off the screen! Change its speed after a few seconds so that it stops center stage. 


Open Loops, drag [pause (100) ms] underneath the sprite’s vx velocity code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

pause(100)

Under the pause(100), add another line of code to change the sprite’s velocity to 0 by typing actorSprite.vx = 0


Inside the parentheses of the pause(100) function, replace 100 with a number in milliseconds that allows the sprite enough time to move across the stage into the spotlight before stopping.


Click ▶ to test your project until the sprite stops in the spotlight!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you customize the sprite’s announcement by updating the parameters with numbers or Booleans inside the parentheses of the sayText function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the sprite say while on stage?

❓ What symbol should be placed between each of the parameters, so that the code is able to run correctly?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the list of potential parameters and each argument’s type, using the documentation box as a guide. Remind the ninja that parameters need to be separated by commas , and strings should appear within quotation marks, in order for the code to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Have the sprite make an announcement when it stops on stage. 


Open Sprites, drag [(this) say (:))] underneath the existing code. Replace mySprite with the sprite’s name. Replace the argument  :) with something for the sprite to say on stage, such as ”That’s all folks!” 


Customize the other parameters for the sayText function: timeOnScreen, animated, textColor, textBoxColor. Inside the parentheses, fill in the other 4 parameters with number or Boolean arguments, separated by commas, to customize the speech bubble. Use the documentation box for help with each parameter.


Click ▶ to see the sprite’s message.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add another pause(ms) and update the argument to a number equal to or larger than the timeOnScreen argument?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the second pause be placed after the sayText code?

❓ Why should the pause argument be greater than or equal to the timeOnScreen argument?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In the next step, a screen effect will be added for the “big finish”. Point out to the ninja that without adding a pause, the screen effect would begin while the text is still on the screen. Help the ninja understand that the effect should happen after the text disappears from the screen.

💡 Emphasize the importance of sequencing to the ninja. If the second pause were placed before the sayText code, then the sprite would be standing on the stage for the set amount of time, and the sayText and screen effect code would run at the same time.
steps.instructions:
Add another pause so that the ending code doesn’t run until the sprite finishes speaking.


Open Loops to add another pause(100) below the existing code. Inside the parentheses, replace 100 with a number equal to or larger than the timeOnScreen argument from the sayText function to give the user enough time to read the message before the big finale.

steps.hints:
❓ Did you choose an effect and update the parameters in effects.blizzard.startScreenEffect

(duration, particlesPerSecond)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What effect might you use to signal the “big finish” of the project?

❓ What type of arguments should be placed inside the parentheses to set the duration and particlesPerSecond of the effect?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If a ninja gets stuck, remind them that the dot operator . needs to be added after effects and before the effect name. This impacts the syntax and affects how the program finds the correct effect to run.

💡 Help the ninja notice the documentation box that pops up to check the syntax of the parameters. Point out to the ninja that both duration and particlesPerSecond take number arguments (in ms). This sets how long the effect appears, and how many pieces will appear on the screen per second.
steps.instructions:
Kick off the big finish with a screen effect. 


Open Scene, drag [start screen (effect) effect] under the // ending comment. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

effects.blizzard.startScreenEffect()

Change the effect by highlighting .blizzard and deleting the text. Type . after effects to open the code completion tool of possible effects. Scroll down the list to the properties then select one that fits the theme of the project.  


The startScreenEffect function takes 2 parameters: duration and particlesPerSecond. Inside the parentheses, fill in the 2 parameters with number arguments, separated by commas, to customize the screen effect. Use the documentation box for help with each parameter.


Click ▶ to see the screen effect appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select a sound for your project in music.melodyPlayable(music.Melody)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of sound might fit the background image, sprite message, and “big finish” effect of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that all of the same sounds are available for use in JavaScript that were available in blocks. The dot operator . opens the code completion tool and serves as the “drop down menu” that appears in blocks, and allows the ninja to add different sounds and effects to the project.
steps.instructions:
Add sound effects to both the set up and the ending of the project.

 

Open Music, drag [play (to play) (playbackMode)] underneath the splash code in the // set up section. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

music.play(music.melodyPlayable
(music.baDing), music.PlaybackMode.UntilDone)

Change the effect by highlighting .baDing and deleting the text. Type . after music to open the code completion tool of possible sounds.


Scroll down the list to the properties then select one that fits the theme of the project.


Follow the same steps to add a different sound effect to the // ending, after the screen effect code.


Click ▶ to see and hear the final production.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Does the code work as expected in blocks?

❓ What is something new that you can do in JavaScript, that you weren’t able to do when coding in blocks?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja make connections between the JavaScript text they have just written and their knowledge of blocks. Ninjas should be very familiar with these concepts already, so encourage them to think about the similarities and differences between blocks and text.
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how are sprite names and other parameters formatted in blocks, compared to JavaScript? Where are the comments?


The startScreenEffect and sayText may have turned into gray blocks. This is because they both have special parameters that are only available when using the text editor. Coding in JavaScript provides many exciting opportunities to customize code.

subgroups.introduction: Create a short show in JavaScript using properties to move sprites and customize sound and screen effects.

validationItems.text: Use a splash screen with a custom message.
Use 1 sprite with a custom name and set its position.
Set the sprite’s x velocity a total of 2 times.
Use the pause function a total of 2 times.
Use the sayText method with 5 parameters.
Use a screen effect with 2 parameters.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about properties and code comments. In JavaScript, you can type directly on the editor to organize your code using code comments and set different sprite properties. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Parameter Pilot
badges.description: Use the JavaScript editor’s documentation and code completion tools when adding parameters to functions.

badges.title: Comment, Like, and Subscribe
badges.description: Add a comment to your code.

badges.title: Say What Now?
badges.description: Use the sayText function with all 5 parameters.

badges.title: Stop and Smell the Roses
badges.description: Use the pause function to temporarily stop your project from running new code.

badges.title: Effective Immediately
badges.description: Use the startScreenEffect function with 2 parameters.

badges.title: Music to My Ears
badges.description: Use the play function to play a melody.

badges.title: To Whom it May Concern
badges.description: Use the splash function to display a message on screen.

badges.title: A Speedy Recovery
badges.description: Set a sprite’s velocity property without using the setVelocity function.

badges.title: Wall of Text
badges.description: Use the showLongText function with 2 parameters.
